note: Recorded GAP. The marking rule is confirmed; the claim that plural traps are designed is not.

heading: Distractor engineering — what can and cannot be said
claim: Distractor engineering is the weakest-evidenced section of the Listening document: the plan asked how recordings set up and cancel wrong answers, and the honest answer has three parts — what is officially confirmed, what published samples demonstrably do, and a recorded gap.
terms: distractors wrong answers set up and cancel weakest evidence section honest answer structure caveat how much do we know

heading: What is officially confirmed
claim: That Listening distractors exist and are meant to mislead is stated only obliquely and by a researcher rather than by the test owners: Field writes that in the case of a multiple-choice distractor 'the text in question is designed to mislead the listener'.
terms: distractor definition designed to mislead who says so not official researcher only field oblique multiple choice wrong option purpose
note: Field, SiLT 53 Introduction. Tier 2 — no test-owner statement exists in this corpus.

heading: What is officially confirmed
claim: On how distractors get into a Listening recording, the Cambridge volume describes only the production route, not the design principle: semi-scripted material 'enables them to manipulate the original text by editing its language and even by introducing MCQ distractors (sometimes with unfortunate consequences for information density)'.
terms: semi scripted recordings how distractors get in production route editing original text introducing mcq distractors information density side effect not a design principle
note: Field, SiLT 53 Ch. 7.

heading: What is officially confirmed
claim: Self-report protocols show test takers feel obliged not simply to seek a match for the correct option but also to disqualify the incorrect ones, which doubles the processing load relative to a naive model of the multiple-choice task.
terms: eliminating wrong options disqualify incorrect ones double processing load multiple choice cognitive cost self report protocols what candidates actually do
note: Field, SiLT 53 Ch. 9.

heading: What the published sample tasks demonstrably do
claim: In the official multiple-choice sample every option is spoken aloud — the shipping agent names all of Economy, Standard and Premium, and separately all of home, depot and port — so hearing an option word is worth nothing; both items are decided by a later utterance from the other speaker.
terms: all options are mentioned in the recording hearing a word means nothing keyword matching fails decided later by the other speaker distractor behaviour sample evidence
note: Description of two published samples, not a stated design rule.

heading: What the published sample tasks demonstrably do
claim: In the official multiple-choice sample the key is delivered by reference rather than by name: the customer never says 'Premium' but says 'I'll go for the highest', which is only resolvable by having retained the agent's earlier ranking, so answering requires holding a scale in memory across turns and resolving a superlative back onto it.
terms: answer by reference not by name superlative the highest anaphora pronoun resolution holding a scale in memory across turns cross turn reference sample evidence

heading: What the published sample tasks demonstrably do
claim: In the official matching sample the answer is the speaker's stance and stance is revised mid-conversation: Jack's five verdicts turn on modality and commitment ('I'd rather do something completely new', 'I'll sign up for that, then', 'anyway I'll think about that one', 'I might wait until then to decide', 'Oh, I'll forget about that one, then') and not on any content word from the course titles.
terms: stance modality commitment will might think about revised mid conversation changes his mind matching keys not content words course titles grammar of intention

heading: What the published sample tasks demonstrably do
claim: GAP — the general mechanics of distractor engineering in IELTS Listening were not established: no official document in the corpus describes how distractors are constructed, and a targeted search of the Cambridge volume for the 'cancellation' pattern (a speaker stating something then correcting or retracting it) returned nothing, with the terms trap, decoy, self-correction and changes his mind absent in that sense; anything a lesson asserts about 'the recording will always say the wrong answer first' is teacher lore with no official or research basis.
terms: distractor engineering gap cancellation pattern wrong answer first then corrected retraction self correction trap decoy changes his mind not found no basis teacher lore generalising from two samples would be invention
note: Recorded GAP. The pattern is visible in one published sample (Jack and Introduction to Cultural Theory) but generalising from it to a design rule would be invention.

heading: What the published sample tasks demonstrably do
claim: An adjacent finding cutting the other way: an item's difficulty is affected by the extent to which its wording follows that of the recording, which gives the candidate an easy indicator of where the answer is to be found and thus rewards the strategic 'key word' technique that crammers recommend.
terms: lexical overlap wording overlap between item and recording makes items easier key word technique rewarded crammers signposts location of answer little discussed factor
note: Field, SiLT 53 Ch. 10.

heading: What Part 4 actually demands — the cognitive evidence
claim: The best single source on Part 4 is Field's 2008 IELTS-funded study of the lecture-based section; it is Tier 2, it is now old, and its conclusions were critical of the format — everything in §6 is a research finding about what candidates do, not a rule about what the test is.
terms: field 2008 study part 4 lecture section caveat age of evidence tier 2 critical of the format what candidates do not what the test is scope warning
note: See the §9 GAP on modern evidence: nothing establishes what changed between 2008 and now.

heading: The model of listening
claim: The Cambridge volume sets out a five-stage model of listening: input decoding, then lexical search, then parsing, then meaning construction, then discourse construction.
terms: five stage model of listening input decoding lexical search parsing meaning construction discourse construction stages process model field 2008 2013 cognitive architecture
note: SiLT 53 Ch. 5, 'a simplified version based on Field 2008, 2013'.

heading: The model of listening
claim: Definitions of the five listening stages: input decoding is linking sensations reaching the ears to the sounds of the language; lexical search is matching groups of syllables to known words (harder than it looks because word forms change in connected speech); parsing retains words in sequence until a syntactic pattern becomes evident; meaning construction converts linguistic form into a unit of information drawing on world knowledge, topic recall and speaker intentions; discourse construction adds the new information to what has been understood so far.
terms: definitions of each stage what is input decoding lexical search parsing meaning construction discourse construction verbatim definitions world knowledge syntactic pattern subject verb object
note: SiLT 53 Ch. 5.

heading: The model of listening
claim: The five listening stages are not strictly sequential — 'the reverse arrows serve to remind us that listening is not a purely linear progression'.
terms: not linear not sequential reverse arrows top down bottom up interaction feedback between stages model caveat

heading: The model of listening
claim: The bottleneck for L2 listeners sits at the bottom of the model: L2 learners have to focus heavily on perceptual processes (input decoding, lexical search and parsing) and so long as that is the case they have insufficient capacity for the rest; Phakiti reaches the same conclusion from the other direction, finding his lowest-ability groups 'could not adequately reach levels four and five of listening comprehension'.
terms: bottleneck L2 learners perceptual processes capacity working memory cannot reach meaning construction discourse construction levels four and five low ability ceiling why weak listeners fail
note: SiLT 53 Ch. 5; corroborated by Phakiti 2016.

heading: The model of listening
claim: The five-stage listening model, not a band table, is what a phonology strand is for: U1-U8 segmental and cluster work is input-decoding training and U9-U12 stress and intonation work sits at the boundary of decoding and parsing — naming the stage a lesson trains is more honest than naming a band.
terms: curriculum mapping phonology strand units U1 U8 segmentals clusters U9 U12 stress intonation which stage does a lesson train name the stage not the band honest labelling

heading: The four meaning-building operations gap-filling removes
claim: Field's central finding about the note-completion format used in Part 4 is that the level of detail and the organisational structure of the notes mean the candidate is not required to undertake four critical meaning-building operations: distinguishing main points from subsidiary ones; distinguishing new propositions from instances of rephrasing and exemplification; recognising the argument relationships that link propositions; and integrating incoming information into an ongoing discourse representation.
terms: four meaning building operations removed by gap filling note completion main points subsidiary new propositions rephrasing exemplification argument relationships discourse representation what the format does not test
note: Field 2008 §3.3.1. Tier 2 critique of the format, not a rule.

heading: The four meaning-building operations gap-filling removes
claim: Field's summary judgement on Part 4: 'The focus of the testing, in other words, is very much bottom-up in that what the candidate has to contribute chiefly takes the form of lexical matching.'
terms: bottom up lexical matching what part 4 really tests summary judgement not comprehension word spotting

heading: Candidates listen for words, not for meaning — with evidence
claim: Field's protocols suggested much of the processing was at a very local level: a number of participants who had scored quite well in the test condition were unable to report the two main topics of the lecture, expand on what the lecturer had said, or trace links between the points made.
terms: local level processing scored well but could not report main topics no comprehension protocols verbal report high scorers empty understanding

heading: Candidates listen for words, not for meaning — with evidence
claim: A candidate who scored 8/10 described his method verbatim as 'my my method to + listen to to do the IELTS listening + yeah I just look at the words not focus what it is about'.
terms: candidate quote look at the words not the meaning scored 8 out of 10 word spotting strategy verbatim protocol quote
note: Quoted in both Field 2008 and SiLT 53 Ch. 8.

heading: Candidates listen for words, not for meaning — with evidence
claim: Correct answers were produced without comprehension: some participants located a correct word without understanding its significance to the lecture as a whole, and two wrote the correct answer 'low frequency' while interpreting it as meaning 'infrequency'.
terms: correct answer without understanding low frequency misinterpreted infrequency lucky right answers construct validity problem word located not understood

heading: Candidates listen for words, not for meaning — with evidence
claim: A counter-intuitive control result: participants identified the lecture's main points BETTER in a free note-taking condition than in the test condition — 'The test method may have served to distract attention from the main points' — and roughly a third found free note-taking easier than answering the questions despite the cues the questions supplied.
terms: free note taking versus test condition main points better without questions test method distracts a third found note taking easier counter intuitive control condition
note: Field 2008 §3.3.3; also SiLT 53 Ch. 8.

heading: Candidates listen for words, not for meaning — with evidence
claim: Field is explicit that IELTS gap-filling is not note-taking: the notes have not been generated by the candidate and therefore represent an unseen text that must be mastered, so the format demands a combination of reading, listening and writing, and 'the test methods used in connection with Paper 4 appear to make considerably heavier cognitive demands upon the candidate than would a real-life situation'.
terms: gap filling is not note taking unseen text someone else's notes reading listening writing combined heavier cognitive demands than real life authenticity criticism

heading: The strategic properties candidates exploit
claim: Candidates rely on the convention that the order of the questions closely follows the order in which information occurs in the recording — a Tier-2 observation of a Tier-1 confirmed convention.
terms: candidates exploit question order convention text order strategy observed use of ordering confirmed rule see section 1
note: Field 2008 §5.1. The convention itself is Tier-1 confirmed in §1.

heading: The strategic properties candidates exploit
claim: Targeted information in Listening is widely spaced, allowing candidates to tune out partially in order to focus attention on the missing word (and its spelling) before tuning in again — one participant reported that while writing an answer the speaker 'was speaking about something else not important for the test', and Field's later analysis confirms items in the IELTS samples are well enough spaced to allow test takers to internalise their content, match it to the recording and identify a response.
terms: answers widely spaced gaps between items tune out tune in write while the speaker continues spacing confirmed not dense back to back items strategy affordance
note: Field 2008 §5.1, §3.3.2; confirmed in SiLT 53 Ch. 10.

heading: The strategic properties candidates exploit
claim: The corresponding failure mode in Listening is a cascade: 'a listener fails to match an item to the relevant piece of information in the text and goes on listening for it long after it is past - thus missing the answers to subsequent items as well'.
terms: cascade failure lost your place missing one answer costs the next ones chain reaction still listening for a past answer catastrophic drift

heading: The strategic properties candidates exploit
claim: A finding that contradicts standard EAP teaching: the two techniques most emphasised in lecture-listening materials — paying heed to prominent items and to discourse markers — were little reported, with discourse markers accounting for 0 instances in one text and 2 in the other, and prominence 1 and 0.
terms: discourse markers signposting prominence stress cues barely used contradicts eap teaching zero instances counts adverse evidence listen for signposting language

heading: The strategic properties candidates exploit
claim: Because candidates in Field's study did not use signposting, it has to be trained into automaticity rather than merely named; and the single-play, widely-spaced structure means the most recoverable skill worth teaching is losing your place and finding it again, which no textbook exercise practises.
terms: teaching implication signposting automaticity not just naming it recovery skill losing your place finding it again re-entry no textbook practises this exercise idea

heading: What separates strong from weak listeners — mostly a gap
claim: Field found NO significant correlation between IELTS lecture-section score and the ability to report propositional content from a lecture heard under non-test conditions (rs = 0.43 and 0.53, both non-significant, N = 13 each).
terms: no correlation between test score and real comprehension propositional recall rs 0.43 0.53 non significant small sample n=13 construct validity
note: Field's sample was small and he says so — treat as indicative.

heading: What separates strong from weak listeners — mostly a gap
claim: Field's clearest process-level contrast is about depth rather than proficiency: candidates 'proved capable of scoring IELTS points by providing the locally-based information that the tests required; but they were not able to achieve what successful lecture attendance would normally demand - a coherent account of the main points of the lecture and the ways in which they were linked'.
terms: depth not proficiency locally based information scoring points versus real lecture comprehension coherent account main points links washback

heading: What separates strong from weak listeners — mostly a gap
claim: Phakiti's structural model gives one usable relationship: state cognitive strategy use had a direct positive influence on IELTS Listening performance (beta = 0.55, R-squared = 0.30, medium effect, falling to 0.36 with difficulty factors in the model), and metacognitive strategy use closely regulated cognitive strategy use (gamma = 0.93, R-squared = 0.86).
terms: cognitive strategy use metacognitive strategy sem structural equation model beta 0.55 gamma 0.93 r squared effect size predicts listening score
note: Relationships hold between latent composites only — see the GAP below.

heading: What separates strong from weak listeners — mostly a gap
claim: GAP — which individual listening strategies help or hurt was not established: Phakiti reports relationships only between latent composites in a structural equation model, there is no correlation table linking a named strategy to a score, and no finding that any particular strategy is counterproductive, so any lesson claiming 'strategy X raises your listening score' is unsupported by this evidence base.
terms: which strategy works named strategy score correlation gap latent composites sem no table not established unsupported strategy claims prediction listening
note: Recorded GAP.

heading: Calibration: the one robust individual-difference finding
claim: Phakiti's headline result is about self-assessment rather than listening: test-takers were miscalibrated in their performance appraisals, tending to be overconfident across all four test sections, with calibration worst for very difficult questions.
terms: calibration overconfidence self assessment appraisal miscalibrated across four sections worst on very difficult questions metacognition accuracy of self rating

heading: Calibration: the one robust individual-difference finding
claim: Calibration specifics: 74% (Section 3) to 86% (Section 1) of test-takers were miscalibrated either over- or underconfident; on very difficult questions test-takers were 25% overconfident (Cohen's d = 0.62) and up to 93% were miscalibrated.
terms: 74 percent 86 percent miscalibrated 93 percent very difficult questions 25 percent overconfident cohen d 0.62 numbers statistics calibration

heading: Calibration: the one robust individual-difference finding
claim: Calibration error runs in opposite directions by ability: many high-ability test-takers (above 70% performance) tended to be underconfident on easy questions, whereas many low-ability test-takers (below 50% performance) tended to be overconfident on easy questions.
terms: high ability underconfident low ability overconfident easy questions dunning kruger direction of error 70 percent 50 percent ability split

heading: Calibration: the one robust individual-difference finding
claim: Perceived difficulty depressed Listening performance (beta = -0.32, R-squared = 0.10, small effect) and metacognitive strategy use reduced perceived difficulty (gamma = -0.52 trait, -0.29 state).
terms: perceived difficulty lowers performance beta -0.32 metacognitive strategy reduces perceived difficulty gamma -0.52 -0.29 trait state anxiety confidence path model

heading: Calibration: the one robust individual-difference finding
claim: Phakiti's own training recommendation is that 'students may be better calibrated by, for instance, receiving explicit feedback on whether they are realistic, overconfident or underconfident'; his sample caveat is that participants were 'mainly Chinese' with a mean IELTS Listening score of 5.71.
terms: training recommendation explicit calibration feedback realistic overconfident underconfident sample caveat mainly chinese mean 5.71 generalisability limit
note: Sample caveat is stated by the author himself; generalisation to a Vietnamese L1 cohort is not established.

heading: Calibration: the one robust individual-difference finding
claim: The most directly buildable finding in the Listening document is calibration feedback: attach a confidence rating to each answer in any listening exercise then show the learner their calibration alongside their score — it is grade-8-appropriate, language-independent, and the only trainable behaviour here with an effect size attached.
terms: confidence rating per question show calibration alongside score cheap to build most buildable finding grade 8 appropriate language independent effect size attached feature spec

heading: Folklore audit
claim: Folklore audit: 'Questions come in the order of the recording' is an OFFICIAL RULE, stated unqualified and for all question types.
terms: folklore audit question order official rule not lore confirmed true widely taught claim verdict all question types unqualified
note: Verdict: confirmed official rule — neither unsupported nor contradicted.

heading: Folklore audit
claim: Folklore audit: 'You only hear it once' is an OFFICIAL RULE.
terms: folklore audit single play hear it once official rule not lore confirmed true widely taught claim verdict no replay
note: Verdict: confirmed official rule — neither unsupported nor contradicted.

heading: Folklore audit
claim: Folklore audit: 'Write exactly the words you hear, don't paraphrase' is an OFFICIAL INSTRUCTION.
terms: folklore audit do not paraphrase write exact words official instruction not lore confirmed true widely taught claim verdict
note: Verdict: confirmed official instruction — neither unsupported nor contradicted.

heading: Folklore audit
claim: Folklore audit: 'Watch the word limit — over-length answers are wrong' is an OFFICIAL RULE, stated twice across two Tier-1 sources.
terms: folklore audit word limit over length answers wrong official rule stated twice not lore confirmed true widely taught claim verdict
note: Verdict: confirmed official rule — neither unsupported nor contradicted. Also in the Cambridge FAQs.

heading: Folklore audit
claim: Folklore audit: 'Underline key words in the questions during preview' is WIDELY TAUGHT WITH NO OFFICIAL BASIS FOUND, and Field documents candidates doing it while treating it as a test-wise strategy that displaces listening — 'it quite often led to a dependence on the written text ... which reduced the amount of attention given to the spoken signal'.
terms: folklore audit underline key words highlight during preview no official basis test wise strategy dependence on written text reduces attention to spoken signal adverse evidence
note: Verdict: unsupported as official practice AND carries adverse evidence — Field's data indicate it displaces listening rather than aiding it. Not merely unsupported.

heading: Folklore audit
claim: Folklore audit: 'The speaker says the wrong answer first, then corrects it' is TEACHER LORE — not stated in any official document in this corpus and not found in the Cambridge volume; it is visible in one published sample but is not generalisable from that.
terms: folklore audit wrong answer first then corrected cancellation retraction teacher lore no basis one sample only not generalisable
note: Verdict: MERELY UNSUPPORTED — absent from the official and research corpus; no evidence contradicts it, but none supports it as a design rule. See the GAP in §5.2.

heading: Folklore audit
claim: Folklore audit: 'Listen for signposting/discourse markers' is a TEACHING CONVENTION WITH ADVERSE EVIDENCE — candidates in Field's study almost never reported doing it.
terms: folklore audit listen for signposting discourse markers adverse evidence candidates did not do it teaching convention counts near zero
note: Verdict: CONTRADICTED BY EVIDENCE in the sense that the behaviour was not observed — not merely unsupported. It does not make signposting useless; it makes it something that must be trained to automaticity.

heading: Folklore audit
claim: Folklore audit: 'Parts get harder as you go' is HALF TRUE — the test instruction wording says so, but the official format page frames the escalation as domain rather than difficulty and observed error rates do not increase monotonically.
terms: folklore audit parts get harder increasing difficulty half true instruction wording domain not difficulty error rates not monotonic mixed verdict
note: Mixed-status row: instruction wording [T2], official format-page framing [C] 3-0, error-rate data [T2]. Verdict: PARTLY CONTRADICTED BY EVIDENCE, not merely unsupported.

heading: Folklore audit
claim: Folklore audit: 'Watch out for plural traps' has NO SUPPORT IN THIS EVIDENCE BASE.
terms: folklore audit plural traps singular plural no support unsupported no evidence verdict see gap section 4.3
note: Verdict: MERELY UNSUPPORTED — nothing contradicts it, but nothing in Tier 1 or Tier 2 supports plurals as an engineered trap. See the GAP in §4.3.

heading: Folklore audit
claim: Field's verdict on washback is that 'Training in using such strategies has come to feature prominently in EAP instruction programmes at the expense of more constructive listening practice', and the volume's epilogue adds that 'Inauthentic listening tasks, including some discrete item formats, have the perverse effect of distracting rather than focusing the attention of the listener.'
terms: washback strategy training crowds out real listening practice eap instruction inauthentic tasks discrete item formats distract rather than focus epilogue verdict why this is a curriculum reference not exam prep
note: SiLT 53 Ch. 12 and epilogue.

heading: Accents and connected speech
claim: Official: 'You will hear a range of English native-speaker accents on the recordings (for example, Australian, British, New Zealand and North American speakers).'
terms: accents range native speaker australian british new zealand north american american which accents will I hear varieties official statement

heading: Accents and connected speech
claim: Field records the IELTS accent set as 'principally British, Australian/NZ, US and South African' and considers IELTS's restriction to standard international varieties 'a sound decision'.
terms: south african accent field accent set standard international varieties restriction sound decision which accents research account
note: SiLT 53 Ch. 7 and Ch. 12. Field's list adds South African to the official four.

heading: Accents and connected speech
claim: Adding a wide variety of accents considerably heightens the demands of the listening task, especially when a single dialogue features speakers of two different varieties and the listener has to switch between them.
terms: accent variety increases difficulty two varieties in one dialogue switching between accents cost decoding demand
note: SiLT 53 Ch. 7.

heading: Accents and connected speech
claim: Word forms in connected speech are highly variable even within a single speaker, varying according to speaking style, context, speech rate, and importance in the utterance.
terms: connected speech variability word forms change within one speaker speaking style speech rate context prominence reduction
note: SiLT 53 Ch. 7.

heading: Accents and connected speech
claim: Speakers take the easiest articulatory route, so 'half-past' might become 'huppast' and 'don't know' might become 'dunno'.
terms: assimilation elision reduction easiest articulatory route half past huppast don't know dunno connected speech examples
note: SiLT 53 Ch. 5.

heading: Accents and connected speech
claim: There are no consistent spaces between words in connected speech, so it falls to the listener to determine where one word ends and the next begins.
terms: word boundary problem segmentation no spaces between words in speech where does one word end lexical segmentation listener must decide
note: SiLT 53 Ch. 5.

heading: Accents and connected speech
claim: Voice normalisation costs time, so item writers 'still need to make some allowance for the need to adjust to unfamiliar voices by avoiding questions which target (say) the first 15 seconds of a recording'.
terms: voice normalisation adjusting to an unfamiliar voice first 15 seconds no questions at the start warm up item writing rule of thumb
note: SiLT 53 Ch. 7.

heading: Accents and connected speech
claim: The word-boundary problem is the accent/connected-speech point to exploit at grade 8: the phonology strand already teaches segmental contrasts in isolation, and the IELTS-relevant upgrade is to hear the same contrasts across a word boundary in connected speech, where the boundary itself is the difficulty — no new vocabulary is required.
terms: teaching implication word boundary exercise segmental contrasts across a boundary connected speech upgrade no new vocabulary grade 8 phonology strand design

heading: Accents and connected speech
claim: Lectures are, in the measured data, the slowest of the common genres — radio broadcasts 160 wpm, conversations 210 wpm, interviews 190 wpm, lectures 140 wpm — with IELTS lecture-style samples measured at 158-197 wpm; Part 4 is not hard because it is fast.
terms: speech rate words per minute wpm lectures 140 conversations 210 radio 160 interviews 190 ielts samples 158 197 part 4 not fast speed is not the difficulty tauroza allison 1990
note: SiLT 53 Ch. 7, citing Tauroza and Allison 1990.

heading: Where the evidence runs out
claim: GAP — distractor engineering in Listening: no official account exists in this corpus of how wrong answers are constructed in a recording.
terms: gap collected distractor engineering how wrong answers are built no official account not established see section 5 target for a later pass
note: Collected restatement of the GAP recorded in §5.2.

heading: Where the evidence runs out
claim: GAP — plural and spelling traps as a designed feature in Listening: the marking rule is confirmed, but the claim that traps are engineered is not established.
terms: gap collected plural traps spelling traps designed feature engineered not established marking rule confirmed see section 4.3
note: Collected restatement of the GAP recorded in §4.3.

heading: Where the evidence runs out
claim: GAP — which individual strategies raise Listening scores: only latent-composite relationships were found.
terms: gap collected which strategies raise listening scores individual named strategy latent composite only see section 6.5 not established
note: Collected restatement of the GAP recorded in §6.5.

heading: Where the evidence runs out
claim: GAP — modern evidence on Listening Part 4: Field's cognitive-validity study is from 2008 and its recommendations (double play, skeleton outlines instead of simulated notes, paraphrase-based items) describe a test that was NOT adopted; nothing in this pass establishes what changed between 2008 and now, so §6 should be treated as evidence about the format's known weaknesses rather than a current description of item-writing practice.
terms: gap collected modern evidence part 4 field 2008 out of date recommendations not adopted double play skeleton outlines paraphrase based items what changed since 2008 unknown currency of evidence
note: Load-bearing caveat on the whole of §6.

heading: Where the evidence runs out
claim: GAP — the raw-score-to-band conversion table for Listening was not established in this pass; no tool may report a predicted band without it.
terms: gap collected raw score to band conversion table 30 out of 40 equals band what score do I need not established blocked no predicted band do not report a band see 01-exam-structure.md
note: Blocking constraint on tooling. Check 01-exam-structure.md for whatever Phase 1 recovered.

heading: IELTS Listening — Format, Mechanics, and What the Evidence Supports
claim: The verification legend used throughout 03-listening.md and 04-reading.md is: [C] = confirmed by adversarial verification with the vote shown (e.g. 3-0); [Q] = Tier-1 verbatim quote from a primary document; [T2] = Tier-2 research evidence about tendencies or cognition, never a rule of the test; [X] = tested and not sustained, where neither the claim nor its negation is asserted.
terms: marker legend tag key confirmed C Q T2 X verification vote adversarial tier 1 tier 2 what does the bracket mean status column evidence grade how to read the markers not sustained

heading: IELTS Listening — Format, Mechanics, and What the Evidence Supports
claim: The source policy is three-tier: Tier 1 (ielts.org, British Council, IDP, Cambridge English) is binding for test facts, marking rules and official samples; Tier 2 (IELTS Research Reports, Cambridge Studies in Language Testing) supplies tendencies and cognitive findings but never rules of the test; Tier 3 prep-industry lore is never a warrant and appears only as the object of a claim.
terms: source policy tiers binding evidence hierarchy what counts as a source may I cite prep books teacher lore not a warrant ielts.org british council idp cambridge english research reports studies in language testing tier three

heading: IELTS Listening — Format, Mechanics, and What the Evidence Supports
claim: The Listening research pass generated 100 candidate claims from 20 sources and put 25 through adversarial verification, of which 21 were confirmed and 4 not sustained — the highest confirmation rate of the six research runs, so format and mechanics are on solid ground while cognitive and strategy material remains Tier 2.

claim: Official guidance: 'You have 60 minutes to read three texts and answer 40 questions. You should spend about 20 minutes on each text.' — the 20-minutes-per-passage figure is often taught as a tutor invention but is printed in Cambridge's own FAQ; it is guidance rather than an enforced rule.

heading: The transfer asymmetry, stated once so it is never confused again
claim: The transfer asymmetry in full: Listening is ~30 min of recording with a separate +10 min transfer window on paper and a 2-minute review with no transfer on computer; Reading is 60 min with no transfer window on paper and 60 min with no transfer on computer.

claim: The no-extra-transfer-time rule holds for General Training Reading as well as Academic: '60 minutes (including transfer time) ... Unlike the Listening test, no extra transfer time is given.'
terms: general training reading GT same transfer rule 60 minutes including transfer no extra time applies to both versions

heading: The transfer asymmetry, stated once so it is never confused again

heading: The grammar ladder — which units actually carry the IELTS value

heading: The grammar ladder — which units actually carry the IELTS value
claim: The syllabus's own priority ordering is misaligned with the evidence: its 'Notes on progression' nominate U11 and U12 as deserving the most practice material, but reported speech sits inside `07` §4.6's GAP (no band-level evidence for conditionals, modality, reported speech, cleft or inversion) while U5 attacks the largest error category at every band and U8 attacks the best-evidenced accuracy discriminator plus the top Vietnamese-L1 omission - so ranking U11-U12's grammar above U5's and U8's is not IELTS-supported.

note: The claim is narrow and stated as such in the source: this is not a claim that reported speech is low-value teaching - it is the national curriculum's target and difficulty is a legitimate reason to build practice - only that for IELTS specifically nothing supports the ranking, and U11-U12's real IELTS payload is phonological.

heading: The grammar ladder — which units actually carry the IELTS value
claim: What the grammar ladder says to train instead of complexity is flexibility - the word that appears at every band from 6 up in both Writing and Speaking GRA - and `07` §8.2's exercise is 'express the same proposition three ways', which at grade 8 is a three-line exercise, not a new syllabus strand.

heading: Syllable-final consonants — the syllabus's largest evidence-backed phonology gap

heading: The arc
claim: Stage 'Now - A2 to B1' (where grade 8 sits): Oxford 3000 backbone with per-unit topic sets pre-taught (~2,000 BNC families is only ~83% written coverage, about 1 unknown word in 6); simple -> compound (U3) -> complex (U7) with articles (U5) and 3SG -s (U8) as accuracy spines; segmental contrasts and onset clusters (U1-U8), word stress (U9-U10), sentence stress and intonation (U11-U12), with chunking seeded as a speaking-task habit from U1 and syllable-final consonants missing and not fixable inside this stage; discourse work is the body paragraph, open -> stand -> close, one turn one subject, and answer then develop.

note: Coverage figures are [V] 3-0; the missing syllable-final-consonant item is [S].

claim: Fast gate check 6: if the artefact teaches templates, model sentences or memorised openers, it fails (checklist B3).
terms: fast gate check 6 templates model sentences memorised openers fail B3 penalised category band 0 band 4
note: Traces to `02` §10.3 and §7 items 1-4 and 21.

heading: The fast gate — seven checks that fail most bad artefacts
claim: Fast gate check 7: every claim must carry the marker it had upstream, unchanged (checklist G2).
terms: fast gate check 7 every claim carries the marker it had upstream unchanged G2 markers inherited never upgraded
note: Traces to `08` §0.1.

heading: Group G — Citation hygiene
claim: G1: every factual claim resolves to a numbered section of `01`-`08`, or to a row in `09`'s own Sources table; a claim with no citation path fails.
terms: checklist G1 every factual claim resolves to a numbered section of 01 to 08 or a row in the Sources table no citation path fails source policy
note: Traces to the research plan's source policy.

claim: G2: markers are inherited and never upgraded, and `07`'s [S/NS] is not the same strength as a [V] or a [C]; anything resting on [S/NS], [T2], [S] or [?] must say so at the point of use, so quoting Banerjee's complexity finding as established fact fails.
terms: checklist G2 markers inherited never upgraded S/NS is not the same strength as V or C anything resting on S/NS T2 S or ? says so at the point of use Banerjee complexity finding as established fact fails

claim: G3: [?] claims - the five Phase-6 verification errors - appear only with the marker attached; citing the g = 0.59 WCF figure bare fails.
terms: checklist G3 unverified claims appear only with the marker attached five Phase-6 verification errors g = 0.59 WCF figure cited bare fails
