heading: Group G — Citation hygiene
claim: G4: Tier-3 prep-industry material is never a warrant - it may be the object of a claim, never its support; 'most IELTS teachers recommend…' as evidence fails.
terms: checklist G4 Tier-3 prep industry material never a warrant object of a claim never its support most IELTS teachers recommend fails folklore
note: Traces to the plan's source policy and the `05`, `03` and `04` preambles.

heading: Group G — Citation hygiene
claim: G5: cross-references are verified against the section they name rather than assumed - four were found broken in this knowledge base and all four are now fixed at source (`07` §1 said §4 and meant §3; `03` §1 said `04` §6 and meant `04` §4.3; `09`'s own D9 said §5.4 and meant §5.3; `09`'s C10 and E8 said §5.3 and meant §4.4) - and any pointer copied out of an older draft must be re-checked.
terms: checklist G5 cross-references verified against the section they name four broken references fixed at source 07 §1 03 §1 D9 §5.4 to §5.3 C10 E8 §5.3 to §4.4 do not reintroduce re-check older drafts
note: Traces to `09` §8.3 item 4.

heading: Group G — Citation hygiene
claim: G6: a claim that failed verification is treated as unproven, not disproven, and its negation is not asserted either; 'spacing has been shown not to beat massing' fails.
terms: checklist G6 claim that failed verification is unproven not disproven negation not asserted spacing has been shown not to beat massing fails
note: Traces to `07` preamble and `09` §0.2.

heading: Summary table
claim: Everything in `09` §2's evidence review is Tier 2: it describes tendencies in learners, not rules of the test, and it may never be quoted as a scoring rule.
terms: evidence review what works everything is Tier 2 tendencies in learners not rules of the test never quoted as a scoring rule summary table
note: Framing rule governing all of §2.

heading: Summary table
claim: Pronunciation instruction has a background effect of d = 0.89 within-group and 0.80 between-group across 86 quasi-experimental studies, but the figure is cited secondhand from a single meta-analysis.
terms: pronunciation instruction background effect d 0.89 within 0.80 between 86 quasi-experimental studies single meta cited secondhand
note: [S] - single meta, cited secondhand; not a warrant for any specific pronunciation product claim.

heading: Summary table
claim: Self-regulated learning interventions report g = 0.72 overall and 1.32-1.39 for achievement across 16 studies (N = 1,780), but the paper's abstract and results disagree and publication bias was detected, so the figure is recorded rather than relied on.
terms: self-regulated learning interventions g 0.72 achievement 1.32 1.39 16 studies N 1780 abstract and results disagree publication bias detected Chen 2022
note: [S] - single meta; internal abstract/results discrepancy and detected publication bias. Cited only in the summary table.

heading: Spaced retrieval — and the finding that should change how we build
claim: Spacing works: a meta-analysis of L2 learning retrieved 98 effect sizes from 48 experiments (N = 3,411) and found spacing had a medium-to-large effect on second language learning - but the numeric point estimate and confidence interval are paywalled, so no specific d for L2 spacing may be cited.
terms: spacing works spaced retrieval medium-to-large effect 98 effect sizes 48 experiments N 3411 point estimate paywalled do not cite a specific d
note: [V 3-0]; verbal magnitude only - the numeric estimate sits behind the publisher's paywall.

heading: Spaced retrieval — and the finding that should change how we build
claim: Expanding review intervals are not better than uniform ones - g = 0.034 (SE 0.0626), non-significant, across 54 effect sizes - and this is well replicated by two independent meta-analyses in two different literatures, which contradicts how nearly every spaced-repetition tool on the market is built; a fixed review ladder is therefore defensible and an order of magnitude cheaper, and building an expanding scheduler is not wrong while claiming it is better is.
terms: expanding versus uniform intervals g = 0.034 not significant 54 effect sizes two independent meta-analyses contradicts how most SRS tools are built Anki expanding scheduler fixed review ladder same day offsets cheaper to build test and explain do not support progressively increased inter-retrieval intervals
note: g=0.034 (SE 0.0626) n.s., two meta-analyses [V 3-0] x2 - Latimier, Peyre & Ramus (2021), 29 studies / 54 effect sizes in subset 2, plus the L2 meta independently. Checklist F4.

heading: Spaced retrieval — and the finding that should change how we build
claim: Interval length matters in one direction only: shorter spacing was as effective as longer spacing on immediate posttests but less effective on delayed posttests, so schedulers should err long (F5) and must never be evaluated against same-session recall (E5).
terms: interval length matters in one direction shorter spacing as effective on immediate posttests less effective on delayed err long never evaluate against same-session recall
note: [V 3-0] from the L2 spacing meta-analysis.

heading: Spaced retrieval — and the finding that should change how we build
claim: GAP: no absolute interval value is established - the evidence says spaced beats massed and long beats short on delayed tests, but it does not say 'review at 1, 3, 7, 21 days', so any specific schedule we ship is an engineering choice and must be labelled as such.
terms: GAP no absolute interval value 1 3 7 21 days engineering choice not evidence-backed label as such review ladder
note: GAP blockquote in §2.1; collected again at §8.1 item 1.

heading: Extensive reading — the strongest content-side evidence we have
claim: Extensive reading produced a medium effect size (d = 0.46) for group contrasts between students who received extensive reading instruction and those who did not, with the conclusion that extensive reading improves reading proficiency and should be part of language learning curricula.
terms: extensive reading d = 0.46 group contrasts Nakanishi 2015 TESOL Quarterly medium effect size should be part of language learning curricula
note: [V 3-0] Nakanishi 2015 meta-analysis; best-replicated intervention in the corpus - six meta-analyses since 2011, all positive.

heading: Extensive reading — the strongest content-side evidence we have
claim: Across 73 studies, 82 interventions and 86 comparisons extensive reading produced a small significant positive effect (Cohen's d = 0.41, SE = 0.07; 0.38 excluding follow-up measurements), with gains across all included language domains - reading comprehension, vocabulary, decoding/fluency, motivation, writing, oral proficiency and general language proficiency - so reading is not only a reading intervention.
terms: extensive reading d = 0.41 SE 0.07 0.38 excluding follow-ups 73 studies 82 interventions 86 comparisons Sangers 2025 gains across all language domains not only a reading intervention
note: [V 3-0] Sangers et al. 2025, Educational Psychology Review 37(4).

heading: Extensive reading — the strongest content-side evidence we have
claim: The two extensive-reading moderators are product features and the most actionable finding in the whole pedagogy pass: limiting learners' text choice to their level gave d = 0.73 (k = 25) against d = 0.22 (k = 57), and including accountability gave d = 0.51 (k = 59) against d = 0.01, non-significant (k = 23) - free, unaccountable reading has an effect indistinguishable from zero.
terms: extensive reading moderators are product features level-limited text choice d 0.73 versus 0.22 accountability d 0.51 versus 0.01 non-significant free unaccountable reading indistinguishable from zero constrained logged reading medium effect checklist B9
note: Moderator statement is [V 3-0]; the magnitudes themselves are [S]. k = 25 vs 57 and k = 59 vs 23.

heading: Extensive reading — the strongest content-side evidence we have
claim: Three limits travel with the extensive-reading numbers: intervention duration was not a significant moderator (β = -0.002, SE = 0.004, p = .669), so a longer programme is not automatically a better one; reading volume was never analysed because 45 of 73 studies did not report implementation fidelity, so nobody knows how much reading is enough; and only three studies included retention tests, with 95% of studies in foreign-language classrooms and 60% in Asia.
terms: extensive reading limits duration not a moderator beta -0.002 p .669 reading volume not analysed 45 of 73 studies no implementation fidelity retention barely tested only three studies 95% classroom 60% Asia
note: [S] - limits quoted from the Sangers et al. full text.

heading: Extensive reading — the strongest content-side evidence we have
claim: GAP: how much of the extensive-reading effect survives in unsupervised self-study is not established, because almost the entire evidence base is classroom-mediated - and the accountability moderator suggests self-study is the harder case, which is an argument for building the log rather than an argument that it will work without one.
terms: GAP extensive reading effect in unsupervised self-study classroom-mediated evidence base accountability moderator self-study is the harder case build the log
note: GAP blockquote in §2.2; collected again at §8.1 item 2.

heading: Vocabulary tooling
claim: The overall effect size for using technology to learn L2 vocabulary was d = 0.64, a moderate effect, from 34 studies with 2,511 participants and 49 effect sizes after Hunter & Schmidt corrections - which must be read narrowly as a defensible upper-bound expectation for digital vocabulary tooling as a category, not as evidence for spaced repetition specifically and not as a promise about our trainer.
terms: technology-assisted L2 vocabulary learning d = 0.64 moderate effect 34 studies N 2511 49 effect sizes Hunter Schmidt corrections upper bound for digital vocabulary tooling as a category not evidence for spaced repetition
note: [V 3-0]; single meta-analysis.

heading: Vocabulary tooling
claim: The incidental-versus-intentional vocabulary question was tested this pass and not sustained, so neither side is asserted; the design-safe default is to do both and claim no ranking, because extensive reading and deliberate study each have independent positive evidence and nothing licenses trading one against the other.
terms: incidental versus intentional vocabulary tested and not sustained X neither side asserted design-safe default do both claim no ranking extensive reading and deliberate study independent positive evidence
note: [X] - Phase-6 panel refutation X3, vote 0-2, logged in §8.2.

heading: Task repetition and shadowing — and a collision with `07`
claim: A 2025 meta-analysis found task repetition has a substantial impact on syntactic complexity and accuracy, with learners producing more complex and less erroneous utterances, and its effects are moderated by implementation variables (task type, repetition type, spacing interval, repetition frequency) and by L2 proficiency - so the parameters of a repetition drill are load-bearing, not incidental.
terms: task repetition meta-analysis 2025 System substantial impact on syntactic complexity and accuracy more complex less erroneous utterances moderated by task type repetition type spacing interval repetition frequency L2 proficiency parameters load-bearing
note: [V 3-0] for the main finding; the moderator list is [V 2-1].

heading: Task repetition and shadowing — and a collision with `07`
claim: The task-repetition/complexity collision and its ruling: task repetition's best-evidenced outcome is syntactic complexity, which `07` §4.2 establishes does not predict IELTS band (complexity peaks at band 7 and falls at band 8, and Kang et al. found grammatical complexity a negative predictor of Speaking score) - so use task repetition for its accuracy effect, which does track the scale via target-like use on named structures, and never report the complexity gain as progress; a speaking drill that repeats a task is defensible, a dashboard showing clauses-per-utterance rising is not.
terms: task repetition complexity collision resolution build rule use task repetition for accuracy never report complexity as progress clauses per utterance dashboard not defensible peaks at band 7 falls at band 8 Kang negative predictor checklist E2
note: [INF] - the two findings are separately sourced ([V 3-0] and [S/NS]/[S]); the reconciliation is `09`'s own reasoning. Becomes checklist E2.

heading: Task repetition and shadowing — and a collision with `07`
claim: Shadowing's evidence is thinner than its popularity suggests: the one systematic review in the corpus (44 studies, 2008-2023) is a narrative synthesis with no pooled effect size and only 15 of 44 studies had a control group, its verdict being that shadowing can help comprehensibility, intelligibility, accentedness and suprasegmental control while research on segmental control was inconclusive - and only two of the 44 studies were judged methodologically strong.
terms: shadowing systematic review Whitworth 2024 Oxford MSc 44 studies 15 with control groups narrative synthesis no pooled effect size comprehensibility intelligibility accentedness suprasegmental prosody segmental inconclusive two studies methodologically strong
note: [S] - not panel-verified. The stronger of the two strong studies (16 learners, no control group) found improvement in comprehensibility and fluency but not accentedness.

heading: Task repetition and shadowing — and a collision with `07`
claim: GAP: no effect size for shadowing exists - there is no pooled estimate to cite and two thirds of the literature is uncontrolled, so shadowing may be offered as a practice activity but may not be presented as an evidence-backed intervention with a known magnitude.
terms: GAP no effect size for shadowing no pooled estimate two thirds uncontrolled may be offered as a practice activity not as an evidence-backed intervention
note: GAP blockquote in §2.4; collected again at §8.1 item 3.

heading: Task repetition and shadowing — and a collision with `07`
claim: The direction the shadowing review does support - suprasegmentals and prosody rather than segments - agrees with `07` §5.2's discriminant loadings (chunking .745, intonation .735 above segmentals .551), and two independent literatures pointing the same way is worth more than either alone.
terms: shadowing direction agrees with discriminant loadings suprasegmentals prosody not segments chunking .745 intonation .735 segmentals .551 two independent literatures converge
note: Convergence note; the shadowing side is [S] and the loadings side [S], so neither is upgraded by the agreement.

heading: Written corrective feedback
claim: Written corrective feedback works: a meta-analysis of 21 primary studies found that written corrective feedback can lead to greater grammatical accuracy in second language writing.
terms: written corrective feedback WCF Truscott Ferris question 21 primary studies greater grammatical accuracy in second language writing Kang Han 2015
note: [V 2-0]; 21 primary studies.

heading: Written corrective feedback
claim: Written corrective feedback is durable: a Bayesian meta-analysis of 52 control-group studies found robust evidence of the durability of moderate effectiveness of WCF over time, so the gain persists past the immediate posttest.
terms: WCF durability Bayesian meta-analysis 52 control-group studies robust evidence durability moderate effectiveness over time persists past immediate posttest
note: [V 2-0]; 52 control-group studies.

heading: Written corrective feedback
claim: The written-corrective-feedback effect is not portable: its efficacy is mediated by learners' proficiency, the setting and the genre of the writing task, so there is no single 'WCF works' effect size to apply to a Vietnamese grade-8 self-study context and none of the meta-analyses studied one.
terms: WCF not portable mediated by proficiency setting genre no single effect size to apply to Vietnamese grade-8 self-study none of the meta-analyses studied one
note: [V 2-0]. Truscott's own position could not be read directly - the cached source page is a bot-challenge stub - so his argument is characterised only through the meta-analyses answering it.

heading: The verdict
claim: The plan's 'descriptors first, question formats second' principle is supported with one amendment: the evidence does not merely permit descriptors-first, it makes format-first look actively counterproductive - but format familiarisation is cheap, bounded and removes a construct-irrelevant penalty, so it stays in the syllabus as a one-off rather than as the curriculum.
terms: washback verdict descriptors first question formats second supported with one amendment format-first counterproductive familiarisation cheap bounded one-off not the curriculum construct-irrelevant penalty
note: [S] - all evidence in §3 was retrieved verbatim from full texts in the research cache and was not put through the verification panel.

heading: What IELTS preparation actually produces
claim: Score gains from IELTS preparation are small: in Green (2007), 476 of 663 volunteers across 18 courses at 15 institutions completed both an entry and an exit IELTS Academic Writing test, with a mean Writing gain of 0.21 bands (SD 0.59) over a mean 5.5 weeks / 130 hours - just three of the 476 gained by two bands or more, only 39 (8.2%) by one band or more, and as many as 31% scored lower on the second test.
terms: Green 2007 IELTS Washback in Context N=476 663 volunteers 18 courses 15 institutions mean Writing gain 0.21 bands SD 0.59 5.5 weeks 130 hours three gained two bands 39 gained one band 31% lower on the second test
note: N=476. [S] - retrieved verbatim from the full text, not panel-verified.

heading: What IELTS preparation actually produces
claim: The published hours-to-band guideline does not hold: score gains fell well short of the IELTS partners' suggested half band per month (100 hours), and even at 200-250 hours 41.5% made no substantial improvement on their initial Writing score, while Cambridge ESOL's own data on 15,343 repeat candidates found those at band 6+ were as a group unlikely to improve their IELTS Writing performance.
terms: hours to band guideline does not hold half a band for each month 100 hours 200-250 hours 41.5% no substantial improvement 15343 repeat candidates band 6 plus unlikely to improve checklist E7
note: N=476 plus Cambridge ESOL data on 15,343 repeat candidates. [S]. Checklist consequence E7 - no artefact may promise a band per unit of study time.

heading: What IELTS preparation actually produces
claim: Starting level dominates everything: the most accurate predictions of Writing score gain came not from course length but from initial Writing score, which alone accounted for approximately 25% of the variance against just under 8% for course length in weeks - and Green names regression to the mean as part of the explanation.
terms: starting level dominates initial Writing score 25% of variance course length 8% regression to the mean best-sourced answer to how long to gain a band is that the question is mis-framed

heading: What IELTS preparation actually produces
claim: Kang et al. (2021) replicate the shape in an EFL setting: 52 learners over 12 weeks with a mean 284 hours of study gained 0.298 bands overall (d = .36), with writing gaining most (0.462, d = .69) and speaking not gaining significantly at all (0.125, p = .185); hours of study explained 17% of gain variance and initial proficiency 22.5%, negatively.
terms: Kang et al 2021 IELTS Research Reports EFL setting 52 learners 12 weeks 284 hours 0.298 bands d .36 writing 0.462 d .69 speaking 0.125 p .185 not significant hours 17% initial proficiency 22.5% negatively
note: N=52, mean 284 hours, 12 weeks. [S].

heading: Does prep raise scores without raising proficiency?
claim: IELTS-preparation courses gave no score advantage over broader-based EAP pre-sessional courses: Green found 'no significant differences between Course Types in terms of Writing score gains', and the only course in the study to average over one band of gain was a pre-sessional EAP course, not an IELTS preparation course.
terms: washback finding IELTS-prep courses gave no score advantage over EAP little support for the belief that IELTS-directed courses are more effective no significant differences between course types only course averaging over one band was pre-sessional EAP
note: N=476. [S] - Green (2007), unusually well designed for this question because he ran independent grammar and vocabulary tests alongside the writing test.

heading: Does prep raise scores without raising proficiency?
claim: IELTS preparation courses produced the least linguistic gain: with covariates taken into account, IELTS preparation students made the least gain in their grammar and vocabulary composite scores despite their teachers reporting more attention to grammar and vocabulary than EAP teachers, which Green attributes to the narrow focus of the IELTS courses limiting learning to items teachers considered test-relevant.
terms: prep courses produced the least linguistic gain grammar and vocabulary composite scores covariates narrow focus limited learning to items considered of relevance to the test teachers reported more attention

heading: Does prep raise scores without raising proficiency?
claim: Memorised formulae are not rewarded: the highest gains were achieved by learners espousing a Meaning-Based Approach, which weighs against the contention that improved IELTS responses can be constructed from an assemblage of memorised formulae - independent corroboration, from 476 learners' outcomes, of the descriptor-derived ban on templates in checklist B3.
terms: memorised formulae are not rewarded meaning-based approach highest gains assemblage of memorised formulae analytic and exploratory approach to learning independent corroboration of B3 and 02 §10 rule 3
note: N=476. [S]. `02` reaches the same rule from the descriptors; Green reaches it from outcomes.

heading: Does prep raise scores without raising proficiency?
claim: The measurement warning that follows the washback data is Madaus': a rise in scores may reflect increasing test-wiseness rather than improving skills, and this will be masked if test scores are used as the index of improvement, so robust designs include at least one alternative measure of the focal construct - restated independently by Field for Listening.
terms: Madaus circularity warning rise in scores may reflect test-wiseness rather than improving skills masked if test scores are the index of improvement at least one alternative measure of the focal construct Field 2023 listening checklist E6
note: [S]. Checklist consequence E6 - our own practice-test scores are not evidence of proficiency gain.

heading: The amendment — format familiarity is not nothing
claim: Format familiarisation is a one-off orientation per question type - what it looks like, what the instruction line says, what the answer key accepts - and is never the curriculum, because unfamiliar formats cause construct-irrelevant variance (an invalidly low score unrelated to English ability), IELTS has more formats to be unfamiliar with than a single-format test, and compensatory strategies must be clearly distinguished from test-wise techniques that exploit loopholes in test method.
terms: format familiarity is not nothing one-off orientation per question type never the curriculum construct-irrelevant variance Messick Winke and Lim familiarization Nguyen 2007 95 participants Vietnamese context listening wider range and complexity of test formats compensatory strategies versus test-wise techniques
note: [INF] reasoning from three [S] sources (Green/Messick, Winke & Lim via Field, Nguyen 2007 via Field). Everything recurring is descriptor work.

heading: Where the washback evidence is mixed — say so
claim: Which skill gains fastest is unresolved - Elder & O'Loughlin (N = 112) found Listening gained most (0.781) and Reading least (0.402), Kang et al. (N = 52) found Writing gained most and Speaking not significantly at all, and Allen (2016) reports the reverse ordering again with a probable ceiling effect - so the design-safe default is not to sequence or budget the course on any claim about which skill improves fastest.
terms: which skill gains fastest unresolved Elder O'Loughlin N=112 listening 0.781 reading 0.402 Kang N=52 writing most speaking not significant Allen 2016 reverse ordering ceiling effect design-safe default do not sequence or budget on it
note: [S]. Kang's time-allocation explanation is the one finding with a mechanism attached, and it points at effort distribution - a product decision rather than a linguistic fact.

heading: Where the washback evidence is mixed — say so
claim: A precision caveat travels with all of §3: Green's own inter-rater correlations were 0.70-0.81 against the 0.85 Cambridge reports for operational IELTS Writing, and he had to introduce half-band ratings because official whole-number band scores make small gains impossible to register - the numbers are the best available and are not precise.
terms: caveat Green inter-rater correlations 0.70 to 0.81 versus 0.85 operational half-band ratings introduced whole numbers cannot register small gains numbers are not precise

heading: Where the washback evidence is mixed — say so
claim: GAP: no IELTS washback study conducted in Vietnam was retrieved - Nguyen (2007) exists in this corpus only as a paragraph inside Field's review and the primary text was not obtained, so every washback number in §3 comes from UK, Australian, New Zealand or Korean contexts.
terms: GAP no IELTS washback study conducted in Vietnam Nguyen 2007 only as a paragraph inside Field's review primary text not retrieved UK Australia New Zealand Korea contexts
note: GAP blockquote in §3.5; collected again at §8.1 item 4.

heading: What makes a band-aligned rubric learner-usable
claim: Three constraints make a band-aligned rubric usable rather than merely correct: one criterion at a time (a rubric asking a learner to judge four criteria simultaneously is a holistic judgement in disguise), observable rather than evaluative wording ('Did you write an overview sentence?' is checkable by a 14-year-old, 'Is your overview clear?' is not), and version-stamping, because two official Writing descriptor documents circulate with materially different wording.
terms: band-aligned rubric learner-usable one criterion at a time observable not evaluative did you write an overview sentence is your overview clear version-stamped holistic judgement in disguise 14-year-old self-applied
note: Builds on `02`'s traceability rule (D1) and output rule (D3); the version-stamp requirement is D2.

heading: Which sub-skills can be validly auto-scored, and which cannot
claim: Six sub-skills can be validly auto-scored: all Listening and Reading item types at 1 mark each provided the official key grammar is implemented; synonym recognition under search conditions; target-like use in obligatory contexts for named structures (3rd-person -s, plural -s, articles, copula, passives); error-free sentence density; presence or absence of named discourse moves (Task 1 overview, Task 2 position, topic sentence, one marker per stage); and answer-key conformity (word limit, spelling, hyphens, two-answers).
terms: auto-scorable sub-skills six yes rows listening and reading items official key grammar synonym recognition target-like use obligatory contexts error-free sentence density named discourse moves answer-key conformity
note: Mixed markers by row: the TLU row is [S/NS]; the rest trace to Tier-1 mechanics in `01`, `03`, `04` and `02` §10.5 and §7.

heading: Which sub-skills can be validly auto-scored, and which cannot
claim: Five things cannot be validly auto-scored: Coherence and Cohesion as a criterion (nothing in the corpus establishes a valid automatic measure), Task Response quality, Lexical Resource 'precision' or 'flexibility', Pronunciation as a band (explicitly forbidden), and pause intent - the judgement of whether a pause is for planning content or searching for a word, which is what the criterion turns on.
terms: cannot be auto-scored Coherence and Cohesion Task Response quality Lexical Resource precision flexibility Pronunciation as a band pause intent planning content versus searching for a word
note: Feeds the not-defensible set for LLM tools (§5.4) and checklist D9.

heading: Which sub-skills can be validly auto-scored, and which cannot
claim: GAP: no auto-scorable format exists for Coherence & Cohesion, Task Response or Pronunciation - only six sub-skills are established - and the most important absence is 'flexibility', the word the descriptors use at every band from 6 up, which `07` §8.2 specifies only as an exercise design (express the same proposition three ways) with no scoring mechanism named; the discriminator we most want to measure is the one we cannot.
terms: GAP no auto-scorable format for Coherence and Cohesion Task Response or Pronunciation most important absence flexibility every band from 6 up express the same proposition three ways no scoring mechanism named the discriminator we most want to measure is the one we cannot
note: GAP blockquote in §4.2; collected again at §8.1 item 5.

heading: The human-rater ceiling — read before believing any scorer
claim: No automatic scorer can be more reliable than the construct allows, and for Pronunciation the construct is very loose: Yates, Zielinski & Pryor (27 examiners, 312 scores) found that less than one-third of the scores awarded to Band 7 samples (29.8%) agreed with the IELTS-assigned score and about a quarter differed by more than one band, with examiners themselves reporting 'If I am confused, I often find myself choosing 6'.
terms: human rater ceiling Yates Zielinski Pryor 27 examiners 312 scores 29.8% agreement at band 7 quarter differed by more than one band if I am confused I often find myself choosing 6 read before believing any scorer
note: [S] - IELTS Research Reports vol. 12; 27 examiners, 312 scores.

heading: The human-rater ceiling — read before believing any scorer
claim: Isaacs et al. (80 test-takers, 8 accredited examiners) found the same structural cause: classification scores were lowest for Band 5 (27.7%) and particularly Band 7 (8.4%), which are exactly the bands whose Pronunciation descriptors read 'shows all the positive features of the band below and some, but not all, of the positive features of the band above' - the bands with no independent descriptor text are the bands nobody can rate, which is why checklist A9 and D8 follow.
terms: Isaacs et al 2015 80 test-takers 8 examiners classification band 5 27.7% band 7 8.4% shows all the positive features of the band below descriptor has no independent wording bands with no text nobody can rate A9 D8
note: [S]; `02` §5.1 records the missing descriptor wording as a GAP.

heading: Learners cannot self-assess accurately
claim: Learners cannot self-assess accurately, which matters because a self-study rubric is by construction self-applied: Phakiti (2016, N = 376, simulated IELTS Listening) found test-takers miscalibrated across all four sections with a tendency to overconfidence, worst on very difficult questions, where up to 93% were miscalibrated.
terms: learners cannot self-assess accurately Phakiti 2016 N=376 simulated IELTS Listening miscalibrated overconfident across four sections worst for very difficult questions up to 93% miscalibrated
note: N=376. [S] - IELTS Research Reports 2016/6.

heading: Learners cannot self-assess accurately
claim: The overall correlation between self-appraisal and actual performance was r = 0.73 (R² = 0.53) - real, but leaving half the variance unexplained - and it fell to 0.54 on Section 4, with the prior literature summarised as low-proficient learners overestimating and high-proficient learners underestimating their skills; Field independently calls self-assessment 'an approximate tool at best'.
terms: self-appraisal correlation r 0.73 R squared 0.53 half the variance unexplained fell to 0.54 on Section 4 low-proficient overestimate high-proficient underestimate approximate tool at best

heading: Learners cannot self-assess accurately
claim: A self-applied rubric is a learning prompt that directs attention to a criterion; it is not a measure, and no dashboard, progress bar or level decision may be driven by one.
terms: self-applied rubric is a learning prompt not a measure directs attention to a criterion no dashboard progress bar or level decision driven by it checklist E8
note: [S], design consequence of Phakiti's N=376 miscalibration result. Becomes checklist E8.

heading: Learners cannot self-assess accurately
claim: GAP: whether giving a learner a checklist or rubric improves their self-assessment accuracy is untested - this is the load-bearing assumption behind 'rubrics a learner can self-apply', and nothing in either evidence base tests it; what is established is only that learners are badly calibrated without one, so a self-applied rubric is a cheap and plausible untested intervention, not a validated one.
terms: GAP whether a checklist or rubric improves self-assessment accuracy untested load-bearing assumption rubrics a learner can self-apply cheap and plausible not validated
note: GAP blockquote in §4.4; collected again at §8.1 item 6.

heading: Learners cannot self-assess accurately
claim: The one calibration finding that is buildable is `03` §6.6's: attach a confidence rating to each listening answer and show the learner their calibration alongside their score - 'the most directly buildable finding in the document … the only trainable behaviour here with an effect size attached' (overconfidence d = 0.62 on very difficult items).
terms: calibration finding buildable confidence rating each listening answer show calibration alongside score most directly buildable finding only trainable behaviour with an effect size overconfidence d = 0.62 checklist C10
note: [T2], d = 0.62 on very difficult items, N = 376. Becomes checklist C10; the pointer for this was corrected from §5.3 to §4.4 (see G5).

heading: The five unverified WCF claims, flagged
claim: Five written-corrective-feedback claims errored in verification (three votes, zero valid) and are [?] throughout, recorded once so later work does not re-derive them as established: that direct, indirect and metalinguistic WCF produced similar meta-analytic effect sizes; that a 2020 meta-analysis of 35 control-group studies reported Hedges' g = 0.59 (SE 0.085, 95% CI 0.423-0.755); that direct (g = 0.761) vs indirect (g = 0.625) was non-significant (Q = 0.322, p = .570) as was focused (g = 0.628) vs unfocused (g = 0.445); that delayed post-test effects (g = 0.569) were essentially equal to immediate ones; and that the result contradicts Truscott's reported d = -0.155.
terms: five unverified WCF claims flagged question mark marker errored in verification three votes zero valid g = 0.59 Hedges direct indirect metalinguistic focused unfocused delayed post-test Truscott d -0.155 recorded once so they are not re-derived
note: [?] - verification attempted and errored; usable only with the marker attached (checklist G3). Appear in §5.1 and nowhere else.

heading: The five unverified WCF claims, flagged
claim: The question 'which type of correction should an automated tool give?' has no confirmed answer in this evidence base, so the design-safe default is to pick the type on engineering and pedagogic grounds - indirect and metalinguistic coding is cheaper to automate and does not do the learner's revision for them - and to state that the choice is not evidence-driven.
terms: which type of correction no confirmed answer design-safe default indirect and metalinguistic coding cheaper to automate does not do the learner's revision state that the choice is not evidence-driven
note: [INF] - `09`'s own reasoning from the absence of verified evidence.

heading: What automated scoring is known to get wrong
claim: The only direct evidence on automated scoring in the corpus is Powers et al. (2001), 'Stumping E-Rater' (27 participants, 63 essays, each scored by the machine and two trained readers): on genuine essays trained readers agreed exactly with one another 52% of the time while e-rater agreed exactly with individual readers about 34%, with reader-reader correlation .82 against .42 and .37 for e-rater, and Cohen's kappa .42 against .16 and .27.
terms: Stumping E-Rater Powers Burstein Chodorow Fowles Kukich 2001 ETS Research Report 01-03 27 participants 63 essays agreement 52% readers 34% e-rater correlation .82 versus .42 .37 kappa .42 versus .16 .27 automated essay scoring baseline
note: [S] - 27 participants, 63 essays. Not panel-verified.

heading: What automated scoring is known to get wrong
claim: The winning attack on the automated scorer was embarrassingly cheap: the participant simply wrote several paragraphs and repeated them 37 times, and e-rater assigned the essay the highest possible score (6) while both study readers awarded the lowest possible score (1).
terms: winning attack repeat several paragraphs 37 times e-rater highest possible score 6 human readers lowest possible score 1 repetition attack gaming adversarial
note: [S]. The failure is asymmetric - it was harder to make the machine score too low, and the two essays that managed it did so through metaphor and literary allusion.

heading: What automated scoring is known to get wrong
claim: A third attack - vary sentence structure, use discourse cue words, use topic vocabulary, and supply no critical analysis whatsoever - scored 6 from the machine and 2 and 3 from the humans; the authors' own limit is that e-rater scores have meaning only if writers make genuine and legitimate attempts to respond to essay prompts, and they flag as unwarranted the assumption that it would be used by itself for high-stakes testing.
terms: third strategy vary sentence structure discourse cue words topic vocabulary no critical analysis scored 6 machine 2 and 3 humans e-rater scores have meaning only if writers make genuine and legitimate attempts unwarranted assumption high-stakes testing by itself

heading: What automated scoring is known to get wrong
claim: GAP: nothing in either evidence base evaluates an LLM as a rater - Powers et al. tested a feature-based system in 2001, and no source measures an LLM's agreement with human examiners, its failure modes, or its behaviour under adversarial testing - so every claim in §5.3-§5.5 about LLMs is reasoning from adjacent evidence and marked [INF].
terms: GAP nothing evaluates an LLM as a rater no agreement with human examiners no failure modes no gaming surface Powers tested a feature-based system in 2001 every LLM claim is INF
note: GAP blockquote in §5.2; collected again at §8.1 item 7.

heading: Where an LLM feedback tool *is* defensible
claim: An LLM feedback tool is defensible on six outputs, each checkable by a third party against a quoted descriptor phrase or a countable linguistic fact: obligatory-context accuracy on named structures ('third-person -s supplied in 8 of 10 obligatory contexts'), error-free sentence density, presence or absence of named discourse moves (overview sentence, stated position, topic sentence), paraphrase and synonym identification, explaining a descriptor phrase against the learner's own sentence, and generating practice items at a specified CEFR level or worked feedback text once a human-defined judgement has been made.
terms: where an LLM feedback tool is defensible defensible set six outputs obligatory context accuracy error-free sentence density named discourse moves paraphrase synonym identification explaining a descriptor phrase against the learner's own sentence generating practice items checkable by a third party
note: All [INF], reasoning from `02` §10, `07` §8.2, `04` §8.3 and §5.2. Explaining a descriptor phrase is exposition rather than measurement and is called the highest-value thing an LLM does. Referenced by checklist D9.

heading: Where it is not
claim: An LLM feedback tool is not defensible on seven things: any band number (prohibited four times over upstream and by A2), holistic judgement of Task Response / Coherence & Cohesion / Lexical Resource 'precision', flexibility (the descriptors' actual discriminator, with no scoring mechanism named anywhere), Pronunciation at all (human examiners agreed with the assigned band on fewer than a third of band-7 samples), pause intent in Speaking, anything at all in Speaking until `06`'s second pass (D7), and raw counts as verdicts (D4).
terms: where an LLM feedback tool is not defensible any band number holistic judgement Task Response Coherence Cohesion Lexical Resource precision flexibility Pronunciation at all pause intent anything in Speaking until second pass raw counts as verdicts
note: Boundary list; the flexibility and auto-scorability absences are §4.2's GAP.

heading: Gaming — the test to run before shipping
claim: Powers' result generalises as a design discipline: any feature a scorer rewards is a feature a learner can inflate without improving - and since the repo already forbids teaching the inflation moves (B3), a tool that rewards them contradicts our own curriculum; the minimum adversarial suite before any scoring tool ships is one good paragraph repeated n times, cue words and discourse markers with no reasoning, thesaurus-inflated rare vocabulary with degraded accuracy, a memorised template with the topic swapped in, and a response 40% under the word minimum.
terms: gaming the test to run before shipping any feature a scorer rewards is a feature a learner can inflate adversarial suite repetition attack cue words thesaurus-inflated rare vocabulary memorised template topic swapped 40% under the word minimum checklist D11
note: [INF] for the suite requirement; the individual attacks are [S] from Powers et al. and [D]/[Q] from `02` §7 items 13, 1-4 and 15.

heading: Gaming — the test to run before shipping
claim: The honest disclosure rule: if we cannot state how often our tool disagrees with a human judgement, we do not publish the judgement.
terms: honest disclosure rule cannot state how often our tool disagrees with a human judgement do not publish the judgement checklist D10 reliability figure
note: Checklist D10.

heading: The rule
claim: The progress-metric rule is criterion-referenced indicators, countable in obligatory contexts and reported as fractions: 'Track target-like use in obligatory contexts for named structures ("3PS -s supplied in 8/10 obligatory contexts"), not a complexity index' - this is checklist E1 and the alternative to the band prediction A2 forbids.
terms: honest progress metrics the rule criterion-referenced indicators countable in obligatory contexts reported as fractions 3PS -s supplied in 8/10 not a complexity index checklist E1 alternative to band prediction
note: [S/NS] for the target-like-use method (`07` §8.2, Banerjee).

heading: Reconciling "can produce a 3-clause complex sentence" with `07` §4.2
claim: The '3-clause complex sentence' indicator is valid as a gate and invalid as a curve: as a criterion-referenced attainment statement it asserts the learner can on demand do a named thing accurately, and since band 4 is defined by 'subordinate clauses are rare' crossing it is a real threshold event; but as a growth index it is invalid, because 'more clauses = higher band' is exactly what Banerjee's data refuses - so a complexity indicator may be a gate (can/cannot, once) and may never be a curve (more/less, over time), and once the learner clears it the metric retires and accuracy and flexibility take over.
terms: 3-clause complex sentence indicator valid as a gate invalid as a curve criterion-referenced attainment statement band 4 defined by subordinate clauses are rare band-5 threshold real event more clauses equals higher band refused complexity peaks at band 7 falls at band 8 metric retires accuracy and flexibility take over
note: [INF] - `09`'s own reconciliation of `07` §4.2, §4.6 and the plan's example indicator; the underlying Banerjee finding is [S/NS].

heading: Five measurement rules
claim: Measurement rule 1: never report our own test score as proficiency - Madaus' circularity warning requires at least one alternative measure of the focal construct (checklist E6).
terms: measurement rule 1 never report our own test score as proficiency Madaus circularity warning alternative measure of the focal construct checklist E6
note: [S], from Green (2007) via §3.3.

heading: Five measurement rules
claim: Measurement rule 2: never treat one retest as improvement, because regression to the mean explains a large part of the pattern in Green's data by his own account (checklist E9).
terms: measurement rule 2 never treat one retest as improvement regression to the mean Green's own account checklist E9

heading: Five measurement rules
claim: Measurement rule 3: measure retention on delay, not in session, because short intervals match long ones on immediate tests and lose on delayed ones (checklist E5).
terms: measurement rule 3 measure retention on delay not in session short intervals match long ones on immediate tests lose on delayed checklist E5
note: [V 3-0] from the L2 spacing meta-analysis.

heading: Five measurement rules

heading: Five measurement rules

heading: What a progress screen may show
claim: A progress screen may show target-like use fractions for named structures, error-free sentence density over time, a vocabulary coverage curve with the flattening visible (so 3,000 to 4,000 does not read as failure), calibration (predicted vs actual, per session), delayed-retention checks on reviewed items, CEFR can-do statements ticked and sourced to a Companion Volume descriptor, and completed discourse-move checklists (overview written, position stated).

note: Mixed markers by row: TLU [S/NS], coverage curve [V 3-0], calibration [T2], delayed retention [V 3-0].

heading: What a progress screen may show
claim: A progress screen may not show any band number or band trajectory (A2), a complexity index over time (E2), a predicted band from vocabulary size or pronunciation features, an accuracy-only line presented as the progress story (E3), or a self-rating as the primary metric (E8).
